messages.subject: number of iindividuals in each detection
parts:
Hello!
I am working in R and I don't know how to integrate the number of individuals of each detection (flock size, for example) in the code.
Here is my code: 
Distance.hn <- ds(data = bd_trans_Distance,
                  key = "hn",
                  adjustment = NULL,
                  convert_units = conversion.factor,
                  cutpoints = cutpoints)

In the help of the Distance package or the ds function I can't find how I can integrate this "flock size" variable in my analysis either.

Thanks for your help!
Alvaro

messages.author: 75e0b0abcbafbc7d
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] number of iindividuals in each detection
parts:
Alvaro

You have animals that occur in groups (flocks). In your data frame "bd_trans_Distance", you must have a column specifically named "size", where you provide the number of animals in each detected flock.

By providing a column with that reserved name "size", the "ds()" function knows to estimate both the abundance of flocks and the abundance of individuals (where estimated abundance of individuals is the estimated abundance of flocks multiplied by the average size of observed flocks).  This estimate is often biased because small flocks at distance are absent from the sample, therefore the average size of observed flocks is greater than the average size of flocks in the population.

This can be remedied by using "size" as a covariate in the detection function.

Hope that helps.

You're right, Eric, I found it in the ds function documentation.

I have run the ds function with 3 different configurations:

+                   key = "hn",
+                   adjustment = NULL,
+                   convert_units = conversion.factor,
+                   cutpoints = cutpoints)
Fitting half-normal key function
AIC= 5497.912
Estimate: 559

2 -) without "size" column:
> Distance.hn <- ds(data = bd_trans_Distance,

+                   key = "hn",
+                   adjustment = NULL,
+                   convert_units = conversion.factor,
+                   cutpoints = cutpoints)
Fitting half-normal key function

+                   key = "hn",
+                   formula=~num,
+                   adjustment = NULL,
+                   convert_units = conversion.factor,
+                   cutpoints = cutpoints)
Fitting half-normal key function
AIC= 5498.913
Estimate: 210

The AICs I've received have been virtually identical although density estimates vary considerably. Does it mean that there are no biases in my data or that they do not substantially affect the results?

Thank you so much!
Alvaro

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] number of iindividuals in each detection
parts:
Alvaro

If you recorded detections of groups, then your data frame must include size; otherwise the ds() function is producing an estimate of the abundance of groups, not abundance of individuals. Therefore your analyses 2 and 3 are not doing what you want (estimating abundance of individuals).

To adjust for possible size bias in your estimation, in addition to method 1) also fit another model:

Distance.hn.sizecov <- ds(data = bd_trans_Distance,
+                   key = "hn",
+                   adjustment = NULL,
+                   formula=~size

+                   convert_units = conversion.factor,
+                   cutpoints = cutpoints)

Perform AIC comparison of those two models to determine if size affects detectability.

El miércoles, 16 de octubre de 2024 a las 18:13:10 UTC+2, Eric Rexstad escribió:
Alvaro

You have animals that occur in groups (flocks). In your data frame "bd_trans_Distance", you must have a column specifically named "size", where you provide the number of animals in each detected flock.

By providing a column with that reserved name "size", the "ds()" function knows to estimate both the abundance of flocks and the abundance of individuals (where estimated abundance of individuals is the estimated abundance of flocks multiplied by the average size of observed flocks).  This estimate is often biased because small flocks at distance are absent from the sample, therefore the average size of observed flocks is greater than the average size of flocks in the population.

This can be remedied by using "size" as a covariate in the detection function.

Hope that helps.
